title: Rehearse a Difficult Conversation with AI Before the Real One
subtitle: Practise wording and likely responses without pretending the simulation predicts a person
description: Before a difficult but ordinary conversation, use AI to role-play several plausible reactions, practise a concise opening, and identify points where you may become unclear or defensive. Treat the simulation as rehearsal, not as a model of the other person's mind.

lifeOsSource.hack: Use AI as a rehearsal partner for several plausible responses, then keep your real conversation flexible and evidence-based.
lifeOsSource.whatYouDo: State the goal, your opening, and relevant context without unnecessary private detail. Ask AI to play a neutral, skeptical, and confused counterpart. Practise responding with facts, boundaries, and questions. Write one shorter opening after the rehearsal and use that in the real conversation if it still fits.
lifeOsSource.checkIn: Am I better prepared to listen and respond, or did I start treating the simulated person's reaction as a prediction?

faq.question: Can AI predict how the person will react?
faq.answer: No. The useful output is a set of plausible reactions that helps you practise. The real person may respond differently and should be listened to as new evidence.

faq.question: What should I avoid sharing?
faq.answer: Avoid unnecessary confidential, identifying, medical, legal, employment, or other sensitive information. Use abstractions when the exact detail is not needed for the rehearsal.

intro.html: Rehearsal is useful because you get to hear your own wording before it matters. The AI counterpart is a practice dummy with vocabulary, not a clairvoyant colleague.

sections.title: 1. Define the real goal
sections.html: Choose what you want from the conversation: clarify, request, set a boundary, repair, decide, or surface disagreement. Do not make “win” the hidden goal if cooperation matters.

sections.title: 2. Practise a short opening
sections.html: State the observable situation, why it matters, and what you want to discuss. Keep the opening short enough to leave room for the other person.

sections.title: 3. Rehearse several reactions
sections.html: Ask for different plausible responses, including misunderstanding or disagreement. Practise asking a question instead of defending every point immediately.

sections.title: 4. Reset before the real conversation
sections.html: Keep the useful wording, discard the simulated storyline, and enter the real conversation ready to update based on what the person actually says.

editorialCuration.reason: Publish as low-risk communication rehearsal with explicit privacy and non-prediction boundaries; not presented as therapy or as evidence about another person's intentions.
